^Ask him to sing of your hero instead

c-0: ^He strums a chord that makes the guards tap their feet. By nightfall the whole valley is humming it.
c-1: ^"A hero! Even better. Heroes rhyme with everything." He leaves already composing.
c-2: ^He sweeps his hat back onto his head. "As you wish. Bards have long memories, Majesty."

b: ^ Lysander is back, and he has brought a crowd. He clears his throat meaningfully.

^ "I have written a new song, Majesty. It is called 'The Miser on the Throne'. Shall I perform it?"
^"Your song is sung from Merrow to Qadir! Kings ask who this ruler is. I came back to thank you."

c-0: ^He bows. "A change of key, then." The new song is about the weather. Everyone is relieved.
c-1: ^The verses are clever and cruel. The children learn them first.

noble: ^A noblewoman in dusty silks stands beside a farmer clutching his cap.
^"This man plows land my grandfather held. I want it back, with the harvest he took from it."
^The farmer says nothing. His hands are shaking.

c-0: ^She presses a purse into your steward's hand. "A wise judgment, Majesty. I will remember it." The farmer walks out without a word.
c-1: ^The hall murmurs approval. Lady Varenne's smile does not reach her eyes. "Of course, Majesty."
c-2: ^Neither is happy. Both bow. That is usually how you know it was fair.

b: ^ Lady Varenne returns with armed riders at her back, all wearing your colors.
^Lady Varenne returns. She is not smiling at all now.
^ "You stood by my house. My house will stand by you. Take this, for your walls."
^"Word has reached me that you favor peasants over blood. Some of my cousins would pay well to see your keep burn."

c-0: ^Twenty gold and a new friend at court.
c-1: ^She weighs the purse. "Cousins can be persuaded."
c-2: ^The guards are glad to do it. Tonight the farmers drink to your name.
c-3: ^She has found another field to argue over. You charge a fee for the hearing.

c-0: ^The villagers watch you do it. They sleep easier tonight, whatever the moon does.
c-1: ^He laughs until he coughs. "Nothing. That is the point."
c-2: ^He goes without a struggle, muttering about salt.

b: ^ The old man is back. This time he carries a forked stick.
^The old man returns, thinner than before.
^ "The desert remembers its friends. I have walked your valley. There is water under the third palm from the well."
^"The wells will taste of salt. I did warn you."

c-0: ^Sweet water, enough for new fields. The villagers call it the Prophet's Spring.
c-1: ^"Give, and keep giving." He takes a loaf on his way out.

^"No taxes, no questions, Majesty. Ten measures for fifteen gold. Half the market price, and the market never needs to know."
^Tell him to try the market like everyone else

c-0: ^The sack vanishes into your stores. Qadim winks. "Pleasure doing business."
c-1: ^The guards seize what he carried. The honest salt merchants send their thanks.

b: ^ Qadim is back, all smiles, with two sacks this time.
^A cart pulls up with a cracked axle and a familiar face behind it.
^ "My best customer! But a little bird tells me the guild is asking where your salt came from. Another deal, and I forget your name."
^"No hard feelings, Majesty. I have reformed. Mostly. Spices, honestly taxed."

c-0: ^He throws in a little extra salt. Silence, it turns out, is salty.
c-1: ^The gossip stings, but the villagers like a ruler who won't be squeezed.
c-2: ^The market smells of cumin for a week.

c-0: ^He nearly knocks over the goblets in his excitement.

c-2: ^He rolls up the chart carefully. "The stars will wait. They are good at it."

b: ^ Ibn Tariq arrives with a bound book of charts and a merchant guildmaster in tow.

c-0: ^The guildmaster pays without haggling, which worries everyone.
c-1: ^Every crown in Ashkara now navigates by your stars.
c-2: ^He bows. "I will name a star after your keep. A small one."

c-2: ^The hall is very quiet after they leave.
